To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The global financial crisis (GFC) had a significant impact on workers' perceptions of job security in Australia.

(i) the financial crisis had a negative effect on job security satisfaction, (ii) partnered workers and those with children were most affected by the financial crisis, and (iii) the financial crisis did not have a negative effect on workers’ employment stability and financial conditions.

(i) job security perceptions declined for workers with a partner, especially if children are present, and (ii) the effects are not explained by the objective measures of employment security and financial conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the global financial crises on perceptions of job security in Australia.
the effect of the global financial crises on the job security perceptions of Australian workers.

the effects of the global economic crisis on workers’ job satisfaction and perceptions of their job security, and in particular the role of family commitments in determining the effects of the crisis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
workers who are overqualified and who are partnered with children, are more likely to have lower levels satisfaction with job security in Australia.
the global financial crisis did not significantly affect job security satisfaction for Australian workers, but that it did affect workers who had more to lose.
workers in Australia did not experience a significant increase in job anxiety during the crisis period.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the global financial crisis did not have a significant negative effect on workers’ perceptions of job security, but that it did increase the anxiety felt by partnered workers with children.
the crisis did not have a large impact on the job security of Australian workers but it did have a significant impact on the perceptions of job security for those who had the most to lose.
workers with children, who were partnered, experienced a significant increase in job insecurity after the crisis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of the global recession on job security perceptions are still present in the Australian economy and are not simply a result of objective economic changes or the recessionary environment.

even though the economy was not in a recession and employment conditions were improving, workers still experienced anxiety about their job security and this was exacerbated for those with more responsibilities.
even in a relatively benign macroeconomic climate, the global financial crisis had significant effects on the anxiety of overeducated workers.
